section.title: The Blood of Christ
section.sectionRationale: Against the backdrop of the earthly tabernacle, the writer proclaims what Christ has done. He entered the true sanctuary once for all by His own blood, securing eternal redemption and cleansing the conscience. As mediator of the new covenant, His death releases the promised inheritance, and unlike the repeated animal sacrifices, His single sacrifice at the end of the ages does away with sin forever.
section.thesis: Christ, high priest of the good things now come, entered the true heavenly sanctuary once for all by His own blood, obtaining eternal redemption and cleansing the conscience; as mediator of the new covenant His death secures the eternal inheritance, and having appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself, He will appear a second time to save those who wait for Him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Christ entering by His own blood to secure eternal redemption and cleanse the conscience; His mediation of the new covenant, sealed by death as a will and a covenant require blood; and the finality of His single sacrifice, offered once for all, awaiting His second appearing.

units.label: Entered by His own blood, eternal redemption

verses.text: But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, He went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation.
He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own {{haima|blood}}, thus securing eternal {{apolytrosis|redemption}}.
For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean sanctify them so that their bodies are clean,
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!

Therefore Christ is the {{mesites|mediator}} of a new {{diatheke|covenant}}, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, now that He has died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it,
because a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died; it cannot be executed while he is still alive.
That is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood.

For when Moses had proclaimed every commandment of the law to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, along with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people,
saying, “This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep.”
In the same way, he sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and all the vessels used in worship.
According to the law, in fact, nearly everything must be purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.

units.label: Once for all at the end of the ages
units.note: and a second appearing to save

verses.text: So it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.
For Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God.
Nor did He enter heaven to offer Himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own.
Otherwise, Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But now He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself.
Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment,
so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.

haima.gloss: Blood. In Scripture blood represents life given up in death. Christ entered God's presence not with the blood of animals but with His own blood, the price of His life poured out, which alone can cleanse and redeem.

apolytrosis.gloss: Redemption, release secured by the payment of a ransom. Christ obtained eternal redemption, a once-for-all deliverance from sin's guilt and power, not a temporary covering but a permanent release.

mesites.gloss: A mediator, one who stands between two parties. Christ is the mediator of the new covenant; His death both ratifies the covenant and redeems from the transgressions under the first, so the called receive the promised eternal inheritance.

diatheke.gloss: A covenant, and also a will or testament. The writer draws on both senses: like a will, the new covenant takes effect through the death of the one who made it, and like the first covenant, it is ratified by blood.

basic.context: Now the writer proclaims the good news the tabernacle pointed to. Christ, our high priest, did not enter an earthly tent with animal blood. He entered heaven itself, once for all, by His own blood, and secured eternal redemption. Animal blood could make the body ceremonially clean; Christ's blood cleanses the conscience. As mediator of the new covenant, His death releases the promised inheritance, and unlike the priests who repeat their sacrifices, He offered Himself once and will return to save.
basic.hermeneutics: Follow the repeated 'how much more' and 'once for all'. The whole passage contrasts the many, repeated animal sacrifices with the single, final sacrifice of Christ. The play on covenant and will in verses 16 to 17 shows why the death was necessary.
basic.originalLanguages: Christ entered by His own haima, blood, securing eternal apolytrōsis, redemption. He is the mesitēs, mediator, of the new diathēkē, which means both covenant and will, ratified by His death.
basic.typology: The Day of Atonement, the ashes of the red heifer, and Moses sprinkling the covenant blood all foreshadow Christ. The earthly copies were purified with animal blood; the heavenly reality is opened by Christ's better sacrifice.
basic.christ: Christ is the high priest who offered Himself, the unblemished sacrifice, through the eternal Spirit. His blood redeems, cleanses the conscience, ratifies the new covenant, and puts away sin once for all. He now appears for us in God's presence and will appear again to save.
basic.god: God required blood for forgiveness and provided it in His Son. It is before God's presence that Christ now appears for us, and God's appointed pattern, death then judgment, is answered by Christ bearing the sins of many.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 16 and 17 tie blood to atonement. Exodus 24 records Moses sprinkling the covenant blood. Romans 3 speaks of redemption through Christ's blood.
basic.oneStory: All the blood ever shed in Israel's worship pointed forward to the blood of Christ, which alone secures eternal redemption and opens heaven itself to His people.

context.literary:
Hebrews 9:11 to 28 is the other half of a diptych whose first panel is 9:1 to 10. Where the earlier verses were built from negatives, these are built from the words 'but' and 'how much more'. The opening 'But when Christ came' answers 'until the time of reform' at once, and the section then proceeds in three movements, each marked by a unit of its own: Christ's entry into the true sanctuary, verses 11 to 14; His mediation of a covenant that requires a death, verses 15 to 22; and His single appearance at the end of the ages, verses 23 to 28.

The first movement is a long, balanced sentence in the Greek, with Christ as the subject and a series of qualifications piling up: through the greater tent, not by the blood of goats, by His own blood, once for all. Verses 13 and 14 are a classic argument from the lesser to the greater, 'if... how much more', with the elements arranged so that blood and ashes are set against blood and Spirit, bodies against consciences, and ceremonial uncleanness against works of death.

The second movement turns on a pun, since the Greek word diatheke means both 'covenant' and 'will', and the writer lets it move from one meaning to the other in verses 15 to 18. The word 'death' occurs again and again, and the third movement then sets this one death against the human pattern of 'appointed to die once', verse 27, so that the two onces, one of men and one of Christ, frame the climax.

The section contains a deliberate rhythm of appearances. Christ appears 'now in the presence of God', verse 24, He has 'appeared once for all', verse 26, and He 'will appear a second time', verse 28. The whole passage moves from past, to present, to future, and the last sentence points to hope: He comes not to bear sin but to bring salvation to those who eagerly wait.
context.historical:
The images the writer uses come from three Old Testament settings that his readers would have known by heart. The first is the Day of Atonement, whose blood ritual was described in the previous study. The second is the ceremony of the red heifer, Numbers 19:1 to 10, in which a heifer without defect was burned outside the camp, and its ashes were kept for the water of purification used for those made unclean by contact with a dead body, Numbers 19:17 to 19. This rite did not deal with moral guilt. It dealt with ritual defilement, and verse 13 uses it exactly so: the ashes 'sanctify them so that their bodies are clean'.

The third is the ratifying of the covenant at Sinai, Exodus 24:3 to 8, where Moses read the words of the covenant, the people promised to obey, and he sprinkled the blood on the altar and on the people, saying, 'This is the blood of the covenant.' Hebrews adds some details to the retelling: water, scarlet wool, hyssop, and sprinkling of the book and the tent. These details are drawn from other cleansing rites, such as Leviticus 14:4 to 7 and Numbers 19:18, and the writer gathers them into a single picture of how blood and water and hyssop cleansed things. Whether he adds from the way the rite was remembered or compresses several rites, the main point is the same.

The Greek word for 'will' in verses 16 and 17 belongs to the world of Greek and Roman inheritance law, where a testament took effect only on the death of the person who made it. The readers lived in that world, and the point would be immediately clear. Verse 22 also reflects the Old Testament's own principle that 'nearly everything' was purified with blood, the qualification being warranted because the law allowed a poor person to bring flour for a sin offering, Leviticus 5:11 to 13, and some items were cleansed by fire and water, Numbers 31:22 and 23.

The writer's language of the 'end of the ages', verse 26, and the second coming in verse 28 would have resonated with a community under pressure. Believers who had lost property and faced reproach, Hebrews 10:32 to 34, needed to hear that the sacrifice behind their hope was final and that the Lord's return was certain.
context.canonical:
The passage gathers up one of the Bible's great themes, that life is in the blood and that forgiveness has a price. Leviticus 17:11 states the principle: the life of the flesh is in the blood, and God has given it on the altar to make atonement. The first Passover shows the same truth in a different key, 'when I see the blood, I will pass over you', Exodus 12:13. Each time blood appears in the Torah it marks the border between death and life.

The prophets deepen the picture. Isaiah 53 speaks of a Servant who bears the sin of many, and Isaiah 53:10 says His soul is made a guilt offering. Verse 12 says that He 'bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors', which is very close to Hebrews 9:28, 'to bear the sins of many'. Psalm 40:6 to 8, which Hebrews 10:5 to 10 quotes, says God did not desire sacrifice and offering, and that 'a body' was prepared. Jeremiah 31:34 promises that sins will be remembered no more, the prophetic goal for which this death is the ground.

The New Testament takes up the language everywhere. Jesus at the supper says, 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins', Matthew 26:28, echoing Exodus 24:8. Paul says God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, Romans 3:25. Peter says we were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot', 1 Peter 1:18 and 19. John writes that the blood of Jesus 'cleanses us from all sin', 1 John 1:7, and Revelation 5:9 sings, 'by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.' Hebrews 9 is the most worked out of these, because it sets the whole sacrificial system in order and shows its fulfilment point by point.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants his readers to understand why Jesus died, and to see that it was not an accident or a defeat but the means God chose. The covenant argument is aimed at a reader who might say: if Christ is so great, why did He have to die? His answer, from the Old Testament itself, is that nothing was ever begun between God and His people without blood, and that forgiveness was never available without it. The death of Christ is not a failure of the plan. It is the plan's centre.

He also means to settle a wavering conscience. A reader weary of repeated rites and unsure whether their sin has really been dealt with is told that something has been done once, completely, and does not need repeating. The 'once for all' of verses 12, 26 and 28 is a pastoral word before it is a theological one. It tells the tired that they do not need to start again.

And he intends to turn their eyes forward. The passage ends not with the cross but with the second appearing, 'to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him', verse 28. The point of the argument is to produce people who wait with confidence, whose conscience is clean and whose future is secure. What the writer asks for is a particular kind of life, one that serves 'the living God', verse 14, and looks for the Lord's return.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes the ritual world of the first covenant and the work of Christ in fulfilling it. It does not instruct anyone to shed blood, and it should never be read as encouraging it. The writer states the old principle, 'without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness', verse 22, as the way the law operated, and he states it in order to say that the one decisive sacrifice has now been made. Churches and individuals who feel they must add sacrifices, penance or suffering to secure forgiveness are doing what the passage says is no longer needed.

The phrase 'nearly everything' in verse 22 shows the writer describing the law as it was, with its exceptions, not claiming a mechanical rule without any qualification. It would be a mistake to turn a description of what the law mostly did into a theory that every act of forgiveness anywhere requires blood, as though God could not forgive otherwise. The writer's claim is about the way God chose to do it, and about the weight of what He has done in Christ.

What does carry forward is the pattern of response. The writer expects that cleansed consciences will serve God, that the second coming will be awaited and that believers will draw near. The passage describes a finished work, and it asks for a life lived out of it, in service and expectation.

debates.question: Does diathēkē in verses 16 to 17 mean 'covenant' or 'will', and why does it matter?

views.label: A deliberate play on both senses
views.case: The Greek word is the normal term for a last will, and the readers lived under Roman and Hellenistic law in which a testament took effect only at the testator's death. The writer moves from 'covenant' in verse 15 to 'will' in verses 16 and 17 and back to covenant in verse 18, using the legal image to explain why a death was necessary to release the inheritance of verse 15.

views.label: Covenant throughout, with a death as the sanction
views.case: Others point out that verse 18 returns to the first covenant, which was no will, and that the Old Testament idiom of 'cutting' a covenant involves a death. On this view the word means covenant even in 16 and 17, and the 'one who made it' refers to a covenant-maker represented by the sacrificial victim, as in Genesis 15.

views.label: Mainly covenant, with the will as a passing illustration
views.case: A third view treats the legal sense as a brief illustration inside a covenant argument. The BSB footnote notes that the word can be translated either way, and the writer moves through the illustration quickly, returning to covenant ratification in verse 18.

debates.bearing: On every reading the necessity of death is the point, and the inheritance in verse 15 comes through the death of Christ. The three readings differ in how they take the Greek and in whether the legal image is a main argument or an aid.

debates.question: What does 'through the eternal Spirit' mean in verse 14?

views.label: The Holy Spirit empowered and accompanied Christ's offering
views.case: Hebrews speaks of the Spirit elsewhere, and the New Testament connects the Spirit with Jesus' ministry from the Jordan to the resurrection, as in Luke 4:1 and Romans 1:4. The phrase on this reading says that Christ's self-offering was done in the power of the Holy Spirit, in a Trinitarian act of Father, Son and Spirit.

views.label: Christ's own eternal spirit or divine nature
views.case: Others take 'Spirit' as Christ's own spirit, the indestructible life of Hebrews 7:16, the divine nature that gave His offering infinite value. The word 'eternal' fits this, and the contrast with the temporary animals is the point.

views.label: The sphere in which the offering was made
views.case: Some read the phrase as the heavenly, spiritual realm as opposed to the earthly and fleshly, which suits the passage's contrast between a tent made with hands and the true sanctuary.

debates.bearing: Most interpreters take the first reading, which fits the Trinitarian shape of salvation elsewhere in the New Testament. Whichever is chosen, the effect is that the offering was voluntary, spiritual and of unlimited worth, and was not one more ceremonial act.

debates.question: Why do 'the heavenly things themselves' need to be purified (verse 23)?

views.label: A figure for the people of God, who are the heavenly sanctuary
views.case: The heavenly things are cleansed insofar as they involve the people who belong to them. The cleansing is of the worshippers and the covenant community, with the language of sanctuary stretching to include them, as the earthly tent's purification stood for the people's.

views.label: Cleansing as dedication or inauguration
views.case: The verb can mean to inaugurate or consecrate, as in the dedication of the first covenant in verse 18. The heavenly sanctuary is opened and dedicated by the better sacrifice, and there is no suggestion of defilement in heaven.

views.label: Heaven has been touched by the effects of human sin
views.case: A third view holds that because the heavenly realm is the place of accusation and approach, as Job 1 and Revelation 12 suggest, a better sacrifice is needed to settle all that sin has disturbed, and Colossians 1:20 speaks of reconciling things in heaven.

debates.bearing: The writer's emphasis is the parallelism: as the copies were cleansed with the blood of animals, so the reality required a better sacrifice. The exact sense of purifying heaven is not explained, and reading it as dedication is the least problematic. It is wise not to press the phrase beyond what the passage says.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 12 says Christ secured an 'eternal redemption', aionian lytrosin. The noun lytrosis belongs to the family of lytron, 'ransom', the price paid to free someone, and in the Greek Old Testament the verbs of this family are used of God redeeming Israel from Egypt. The adjective aionios, 'eternal', is placed in the emphatic position at the head of the phrase, so that the writer insists the redemption was not for a season. The verb 'securing', heuramenos, literally 'having found', is a middle participle: Christ found this redemption for Himself and for us at the cost of His own life.

Verse 14 calls Christ 'unblemished', amomon. The word is the standard Greek for an animal without defect, the kind the law demanded, and Peter uses the related word amomos when he says we were redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, 'a lamb without blemish or spot', 1 Peter 1:19. The writer takes a sacrificial word and applies it to a person, and then adds that He offered Himself 'to God', so that the offering is directed Godward and not simply toward the sinner. The verb for 'purify', katharizo, is the same cleansing used for the leper and the vessel in the old law, and here its object is the conscience, syneidesis, the inner witness that the old gifts could not touch.

The phrase 'works of death', nekron erga, is literally 'dead works', which can mean works that issue in death or works that are lifeless. The writer repeats it in Hebrews 6:1, where 'repentance from dead works' is a first principle. Whatever its exact sense, it names what the conscience carries and what Christ's blood removes, so that the cleansed person is free to 'serve', latreuo, the living God. This is the same verb as the old sacred service in 9:9, so the worship that the old system could not perfect is now made possible.

Verses 16 and 17 use the word diathemenos, 'the one who made it', the testator, and bebaia, 'firm' or 'valid', for a will in force over the dead. The pun on diatheke is the best known feature of the section, but it should be seen against the verb in verse 18, enkekainistai, 'inaugurated' or 'dedicated', the word from which we get the idea of a dedication. The first covenant was dedicated by blood. The verse adds that this was not a mere formality, since a covenant that was dedicated in blood could not be withdrawn lightly.

Verse 22 says 'without the shedding of blood', haimatekchysia, a compound noun that literally means pouring out of blood. The word for 'forgiveness' is aphesis, release, the same word Jesus uses at the supper when He says His blood is poured out 'for the forgiveness of sins', Matthew 26:28. The consonance is deliberate. The writer's phrase is a statement of the pattern, and Jesus' words claim it.

Verse 24 says the earthly sanctuary was a copy, antitypos, of the true one. Notice that in chapter 8 the word was hypodeigma, 'example', and here antitypos, 'copy' or 'counterpart', a word that means something that stands over against its pattern. In verse 24 Christ appears, emphanizo, 'to be made visible', 'in the presence of God', literally before the face of God. Verse 26 says He 'appeared', pephanerotai, and that He did so to bring about the athetesis of sin, 'the setting aside' or 'annulment', a legal word for cancelling a decree. The phrase 'end of the ages', synteleia ton aionon, speaks of the convergence of the ages, the point where they meet and are completed.

Verse 28 says Christ was offered 'to bear', anenenkein, the sins of many. This is the verb of Isaiah 53:12 in the Greek Old Testament, and Peter uses it when he says that Christ bore our sins 'in His body on the tree', 1 Peter 2:24. It means to carry up, to lift as a load to an altar, and the writer says that He will appear again 'not to bear sin', the same verb negated. Those who 'eagerly await' Him are apekdechomenoi, a compound that carries the idea of waiting with expectation and is used in Romans 8:23 and 25 and in Philippians 3:20 of the believer's hope.

typology.type: The red heifer's ashes and the water of purification, Numbers 19
typology.fulfillment: The heifer was without defect, was killed outside the camp, and its ashes were used for cleansing the unclean, Numbers 19:2 to 9. Hebrews says that if that could make bodies ceremonially clean, Christ's blood does much more, purifying consciences, verses 13 and 14. Hebrews 13:12 notes that Jesus also suffered 'outside the city gate' to sanctify the people by His own blood. The type corresponds in a victim without blemish, a death outside the camp, and a cleansing of the defiled, and it falls short in that its effect was external and temporary, where Christ's is inward and permanent.

typology.type: Moses sprinkling the blood of the covenant, Exodus 24:6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai Moses sprinkled blood and said, 'This is the blood of the covenant', Exodus 24:8. At the last supper Jesus used the same words, 'This is My blood of the covenant', Matthew 26:28, and Hebrews 9:15 to 20 treats the death of Christ as the inaugurating act of the new covenant. The correspondence is exact in form: a covenant, a word, blood. The escalation is that the animal blood sealed a promise the people could not keep, while Christ's blood sealed a covenant in which God supplies what He asks. The type is partial in that it set a people apart without changing their hearts.

typology.type: The Day of Atonement, the high priest carrying blood through the veil, verses 7, 12 and 25
typology.fulfillment: Every year the high priest took blood into the inner room, but never his own, and left again. Christ entered 'the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood', verse 12, and He did not enter a man-made copy but heaven itself, verse 24. The pattern is the same in structure, a priest, a veil, blood and an entry, and different in everything else: one entry instead of many, His own blood instead of another's, and heaven in place of a tent. The type fails only by its repetition, which in Hebrews 10:3 is itself the evidence that sins were not finally removed.

typology.type: The appointed single death and judgment as a pattern for Christ's single offering, verses 27 and 28
typology.fulfillment: The writer sets a human pattern beside the work of Christ: man dies once and faces judgment, and Christ was offered once and will appear a second time. This is an analogy by form, not a type in the strict sense. The correspondence is of 'once', and the difference is in the result. The judgment that follows human death is met in Christ by one who has already borne the sins of many, Isaiah 53:12. The analogy falls short in that Christ's death is not simply an instance of the human rule but the means by which that rule's final consequence is removed for those who await Him.

study.christ:
This chapter says more about what Christ did than almost any other, and it speaks with the vocabulary of every Old Testament offering. He is priest and sacrifice, mediator and testator, the One who goes in and the One who comes out again. Each of these roles answers a particular need left open by the earthly tent.

First, He is the priest who goes through a greater tent, verse 11. The writer calls it 'not made by hands', which is not a way of saying it is imaginary. It is the sanctuary where God actually is, and Christ has gone into it. Verse 24 says He appears there 'now' on our behalf. The priest is not offstage. He is in the presence of God at this moment, and He is there for us.

Second, He is the offering. 'He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood', verse 12. The high priest took blood that belonged to another. Christ carries His own. The writer adds in verse 14 that He 'offered Himself unblemished to God', and that He did it 'through the eternal Spirit'. No one took His life from Him, as John 10:18 says. It was a priestly act freely done, and it had the weight of the whole divine life behind it. That is why it is enough.

Third, He is the mediator and the testator. A will takes effect at death, and an inheritance needs a death to release it. Verse 15 says that through His death 'those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance'. The covenant that Jeremiah promised could not be enacted without Him dying, and Luke 22:20 shows Him saying so over the cup. The death is not an obstacle to the plan. It is its hinge.

Fourth, His work is final. Three times the passage says 'once', in 12, 26 and 28. The entry is once, the appearance is once, the offering is once. This is the theme of Romans 6:10, 1 Peter 3:18 and Hebrews 10:10 and 14. Nothing needs to be added, and nothing can be taken away. A single sacrifice is not too little, because of who offered it.

Fifth, He is coming back. 'He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation', verse 28. The first appearing dealt with sin, and the second brings its fruit. In the old ritual, the people waited outside while the high priest was in the inner room, watching for his return. Here the waiting people look for the One who has gone in on their behalf. Titus 2:13 calls it 'the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ'.

The links here are those the New Testament makes. The writer does not claim every detail of the red heifer or the scarlet wool is a coded picture of the cross. He draws on the principle that blood ratifies a covenant, that a spotless victim is offered, that a priest enters with blood and comes out. The pattern holds because the New Testament itself uses it, and what Hebrews adds is the demonstration that, in Jesus, all of it has been done once and for all.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who has ordered forgiveness around a costly gift, and who has Himself paid. The writer's statement that 'without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness', verse 22, can sound like a harsh price, but it is followed at once by the account of who pays it. God does not demand a death from the people and leave them to find it. He provides the offering. Romans 3:25 says God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice, and 2 Corinthians 5:19 says God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ. The One who requires the sacrifice is the One who supplies it.

It shows a God who is holy and whose holiness is not set aside by kindness. Forgiveness is never presented here as God simply deciding to overlook sin. The writer says there must be a death, because sin is real and judgment is real, as verse 27 reminds us. The justice of God is not dissolved. It is met. Hebrews 9:15 says Christ died to redeem people from transgressions under the first covenant, which means that even the forgiveness given before the cross was given on the credit of this death, a point Paul makes in Romans 3:25 and 26 when he says God passed over sins in His forbearance.

It shows a God who works as a Trinity in salvation. The writer says Christ offered Himself 'through the eternal Spirit' 'to God', verse 14. The Son offers, the Father receives, and the Spirit is involved in the offering. The pattern fits the picture throughout the New Testament of one divine plan carried out by three persons, and it is more than a doctrinal formula here, because it explains why the offering has infinite value.

It shows a God who is faithful to His promises across the covenants. The inheritance in verse 15 is 'promised', and the covenant of Jeremiah is ratified in a way that matches how the first was ratified at Sinai. God does not change method arbitrarily. He keeps to the pattern of blood and covenant and fulfils it. And He is faithful in the end: the one who comes again 'to bring salvation' is the same God who made the promise.

It shows a God who sets a limit to time. There is a 'foundation of the world', verse 26, and an 'end of the ages', and God has acted at the turning point. The appointed pattern of death and judgment, verse 27, is also His. He is Lord of the calendar of history, and His decisive act is not repeated.

For worship, the passage invites gratitude without anxiety. The God who asked for blood gave it, and so the conscience can be quiet. The right response is the one the passage names: to 'serve the living God', verse 14. A cleansed conscience is not an end in itself. It frees the person to worship.

crossReferences.note: Moses sprinkles the blood on the altar and the people, saying 'This is the blood of the covenant'. Hebrews 9:19 and 20 retells it to show that even the first covenant was inaugurated with blood, and Jesus' words at the supper in Matthew 26:28 pick up the same phrase.

The principle behind all the sacrifices: the life of the flesh is in the blood, and God has given it on the altar to make atonement. It shows that blood is not a ritual accident, and it is the root of verse 22's statement about the shedding of blood.

The high priest brings the blood of the goat for the people behind the veil and sprinkles it on the mercy seat, making atonement for the Most Holy Place. This is the rite of verses 7 and 25, and the point of comparison for Christ's entry with His own blood.

The ashes of the red heifer are kept for the water of purification, 'for purification from sin'. It is the second Old Testament rite Hebrews 9:13 names, and shows that the cleansing of the body by outward means is what the law could do.

The Servant's soul is made a guilt offering, He bears the iniquities of many and makes intercession for the transgressors. Hebrews 9:28 borrows the phrase 'bear the sin of many', and so ties Christ's death to the Servant who gives His life in the place of others.

God does not require sacrifice and offering, but the speaker says 'Here I am, I have come'. Hebrews 10:5 to 10 reads it as the voice of Christ, and it explains why His offering is not one more sacrifice but a doing of God's will, which stands behind the 'offered Himself' of 9:14.

Paul says believers are justified through the redemption in Christ and that God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood. It uses the same words for redemption and mercy seat as Hebrews 9, and shows Paul and the writer teaching the same doctrine.

We were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot. It gives the same sacrificial picture as 'unblemished' in verse 14, and applies it to the way believers should live.

Jesus at the supper: 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins'. It joins the Sinai words, the many of Isaiah 53, and forgiveness, and so supplies the point from which Hebrews 9:15 to 22 reasons.

The conclusion drawn from this passage: believers have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all, and by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being made holy. It repeats 'once for all' and shows what it means for daily life.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning of the Bible, a gap opens between a holy God and a people who are not, and every attempt to cross it involves a cost. In Genesis 3 God covers the pair with skins, which implies a death. Abel brings an offering from his flock and God regards it. On the night of the exodus the lambs' blood marks the doors, Exodus 12:13, and at Sinai the covenant is made in blood, Exodus 24:8. The tabernacle then arranges the whole thing into a system, with daily offerings, an annual Day of Atonement, and a standing reminder that sin is deadly and that God has provided a way to live.

The system worked as God designed it to work, and it also pointed beyond itself. The prophets knew that animal blood could not do everything, and Psalm 40:6 says God did not require burnt offerings and sin offerings. Isaiah saw a Servant whose life was the offering. Jeremiah heard of a covenant under which sins would not be remembered. The sacrifices kept the hope alive, and Hebrews says the repeated rites could never take away sin, 10:4, but they also trained a nation to see what a real solution would require.

Hebrews 9:11 to 28 tells how the promise was kept. Christ is both the priest who enters and the blood that opens the way, and the offering that was repeated over centuries is made once. All the earlier blood, from the skins of Eden to the lambs of Passover to the goats of the Day of Atonement, finds its meaning in the one who actually deals with sin. The covenant that was sealed at Sinai and broken is replaced by one sealed in a death that God Himself provided.

The story is not finished at the cross. The second half of verse 28 looks forward to a second appearing, and Romans 8:23 says that creation and believers still wait for the redemption of bodies. The 'eternal inheritance' of verse 15 is held in promise now and given in full then. Revelation sets the end beside the beginning: the Lamb who was slain is worshipped, Revelation 5:9, and the people redeemed by His blood stand before the throne. The story that began with a closed garden and a flaming sword ends with an open city, and the way in is the blood that was shed once.

quiz.q: How did Christ enter the true sanctuary, and what did He secure?

options.text: By His own blood, once for all, securing eternal redemption.
By the blood of goats and calves, year after year.
options.note: That was the old system; Christ entered by His own blood.

options.text: By His own blood, entering heaven itself for us.
options.note: True and central, and the passage adds that He did so once for all, securing eternal redemption.

options.text: By His own blood, but only a temporary covering.
options.note: It was not temporary; He secured eternal redemption.

quiz.q: What can the blood of Christ do that animal blood could not?

options.text: Purify the conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
options.note: Verse 14 contrasts inward cleansing with mere ceremonial cleanness.

options.text: Only make the body ceremonially clean.
options.note: That is what animal blood did; Christ's blood cleanses the conscience.

options.text: Nothing more than the old sacrifices.
options.note: His blood accomplishes far more, cleansing within.

options.text: Secure an eternal, not merely yearly, redemption.
options.note: True, His redemption is eternal; here the specific contrast is that His blood purifies the conscience, which animal blood could not.

quiz.q: Why does the writer say the new covenant required a death?

options.text: Because a will takes effect only at the death of the one who made it, and a covenant is ratified by blood.
options.note: Verses 16 to 18 make this argument on both senses of diathēkē.

options.text: Because death is meaningless in covenants.
options.note: Death is essential; without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.

options.text: Because without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.
options.note: This is a true principle from verse 22, applied here through the double sense of covenant and will, which required Christ's own death.
Animal blood ratified the first covenant, but the new required Christ's own death.

quiz.q: What does the passage say about the number of times Christ was offered?

options.text: Once for all at the end of the ages, and He will appear a second time to save.
options.note: Verses 26 to 28 stress the single sacrifice and the second appearing.

options.text: Repeatedly, like the yearly high priest.
options.note: Unlike the yearly priest, Christ was offered once for all.

options.text: Twice, once for sin and once again for sin.
options.note: He was offered once for sin; His second appearing is not to bear sin but to save.

options.text: Once, so that no further offering for sin is ever needed.
options.note: True regarding the single offering, though the fuller answer adds that He will appear a second time to bring salvation.

questions: Christ's blood cleanses the conscience, not just the body. What guilt do you need to bring to that cleansing rather than trying to bury it?
A cleansed conscience is given so that we may serve the living God. How does freedom from guilt free you to serve joyfully?
Christ now appears in God's presence on your behalf. How does His present, personal representation of you change how you pray and live?
His sacrifice was once for all, never to be repeated. Where are you tempted to think you must add to what Christ has already finished?
He will appear a second time to save those who wait for Him. How does eagerly awaiting His return shape your priorities this week?

translationNotes.note: The word diathēkē means both covenant and will; verses 16 to 17 shift to the sense of a last will, whose provisions take effect only upon the death of the one who made it.
'Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness' summarizes the sacrificial principle of the law; 'nearly everything' allows for exceptions such as certain grain or money offerings.
'To bear the sins of many' echoes Isaiah 53:12; the 'second time' introduces the New Testament theme of Christ's return, here framed as bringing salvation rather than dealing with sin.
